abstracts.abstract: We introduce a fundamentally new security model for lattice-based cryptographic primitives that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between pre-quantum and post-quantum security guarantees. Traditional security analyses treat lattice problems as static mathematical entities, failing to capture the adaptive nature of quantum adversaries. Our framework, termed Adaptive Quantum Security (AQS), models cryptographic schemes as evolving systems where security properties dynamically interact with computational complexity classes under quantum attack scenarios. We prove that under AQS, standard lattice assumptions—including the Learning With Errors (LWE) and Ring-LWE problems—exhibit qualitatively different security profiles compared to classical reductionist proofs. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain lattice-based signatures achieve unconditional security against quantum chosen-message attacks, provided the underlying trapdoor functions satisfy a novel consistency property we introduce. Our analysis reveals that previous provable security treatments of lattice cryptography contained implicit assumptions incompatible with quantum information theory. This work establishes a new paradigm for post-quantum cryptography where security proofs must account for quantum measurement disturbance in cryptographic state, fundamentally altering how we construct and analyze post-quantum schemes. We provide explicit constructions achieving AQS security and prove their efficiency remains polynomial-time equivalent to existing lattice-based systems.

We present a comprehensive analysis that yields substantially tighter security reductions for elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocols, improving the state-of-the-art by a factor of quadratic speedup in reduction tightness. The elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) forms the foundation of modern key exchange, yet existing provable security treatments suffer from significant gaps between theoretical guarantees and practical security levels. Our approach introduces a novel algebraic framework for analyzing elliptic curve group structures that exploits subtle properties of endomorphism rings in cryptographically relevant curves. We prove that the ECDLP on prime-order subgroups of elliptic curves over finite fields requires at least Ω(√n) operations for curves with embedding degree suitable for pairing-based protocols, where n denotes the subgroup order. This represents a 50% improvement in the exponent of the lower bound compared to previous results. Furthermore, we establish new upper bounds on the advantages of index calculus attacks against structured subgroups, demonstrating that generic subgroup confinement provides provable protection beyond what was previously established. Our analysis directly translates to improved parameter recommendations for elliptic curve cryptography, enabling more efficient implementations while maintaining equivalent or superior security margins. We provide concrete guidance for curve selection that balances security, performance, and implementation simplicity.

We introduce a novel cryptographic protocol architecture that enables composable secure multi-party computation through an entirely new paradigm: homomorphic consensus-based computation. Traditional approaches to secure multi-party computation rely on problem-specific circuit representations, leading to substantial overhead for complex functionalities. Our construction, H-Compose, replaces traditional garbled circuits and secret sharing schemes with a unified framework based on threshold homomorphic encryption combined with a novel consensus mechanism that operates directly on encrypted data. The protocol allows n parties to jointly evaluate arbitrary polynomial-time functions on their private inputs while revealing only the function output, with security guaranteed against any t < n/2 malicious adversaries under our new UC-Hom security model. We implement a complete prototype and demonstrate its practical applicability through benchmark evaluations on standard multi-party computation tasks including private set intersection, secure auctions, and machine learning inference. Our system achieves communication complexity O(n² · κ · log N), where κ represents the security parameter and N denotes the input domain size—representing a qualitative improvement over existing solutions for high-latency network scenarios. The protocol introduces a novel combination of verifiable homomorphic encryption with distributed key generation that enables efficient abort detection and fairness guarantees without sacrificing privacy. This work fundamentally reimagines the boundary between multi-party computation and distributed consensus, opening new directions for cryptographic protocol design.

We present an optimized implementation of hash-based digital signature schemes achieving order-of-magnitude performance improvements over existing solutions while maintaining strong security guarantees. The proliferation of quantum computing threats has renewed interest in hash-based signatures as a post-quantum alternative, yet practical deployment remains hindered by bandwidth and latency overhead. Our construction, HORST-X, builds upon the HORST proposal but introduces three key innovations: a novel tree traversal algorithm reducing signature size by 38% through intelligent node aggregation, a parallelized verification strategy exploiting SIMD instructions to achieve 4.2× speedup, and a reduced public key format enabling seamless integration with existing certificate infrastructure. We provide rigorous security proofs under the random oracle model, establishing tightness bounds for collision resistance of the underlying hash function. Implementation results demonstrate signing at 285,000 operations per second on commodity AVX2 hardware and verification at 890,000 operations per second, representing the fastest published hash-based signature implementation for the 128-bit security level. The scheme operates within 2.4 KB signature size with 32-byte public keys, making it particularly suitable for constrained IoT environments and certificate chains where bandwidth optimization is critical. Side-channel analysis confirms resistance to timing and power consumption attacks under standard assumptions, and we provide explicit countermeasures against cache-timing vulnerabilities affecting previous hash-based constructions.
